play.title: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second

description: The coast of Wales. A castle in view.

entries.text: Drums; flourish and colours. Enter KING RICHARD II, the BISHOP OF CARLISLE, DUKE OF AUMERLE, and Soldiers
Barkloughly castle call they this at hand?
sourceLines: Barkloughly castle call they this at hand?

entries.text: Yea, my lord.
sourceLines: Yea, my lord. How brooks your grace the air,

entries.text: How brooks your grace the air, After your late tossing on the breaking seas?
sourceLines: Yea, my lord. How brooks your grace the air,
After your late tossing on the breaking seas?

entries.text: Needs must I like it well: I weep for joy To stand upon my kingdom once again.
sourceLines: Needs must I like it well: I weep for joy
To stand upon my kingdom once again.

entries.text: Dear earth, I do salute thee with my hand, Though rebels wound thee with their horses' hoofs:
sourceLines: Dear earth, I do salute thee with my hand,
Though rebels wound thee with their horses' hoofs:

entries.text: As a long-parted mother with her child Plays fondly with her tears and smiles in meeting, So, weeping, smiling, greet I thee, my earth, And do thee favours with my royal hands.
sourceLines: As a long-parted mother with her child
Plays fondly with her tears and smiles in meeting,
So, weeping, smiling, greet I thee, my earth,
And do thee favours with my royal hands.

entries.text: Feed not thy sovereign's foe, my gentle earth, Nor with thy sweets comfort his ravenous sense;
sourceLines: Feed not thy sovereign's foe, my gentle earth,
Nor with thy sweets comfort his ravenous sense;

entries.text: But let thy spiders, that suck up thy venom, And heavy-gaited toads lie in their way, Doing annoyance to the treacherous feet Which with usurping steps do trample thee:
sourceLines: But let thy spiders, that suck up thy venom,
And heavy-gaited toads lie in their way,
Doing annoyance to the treacherous feet
Which with usurping steps do trample thee:

entries.text: Yield stinging nettles to mine enemies;
sourceLines: Yield stinging nettles to mine enemies;

entries.text: And when they from thy bosom pluck a flower, Guard it, I pray thee, with a lurking adder Whose double tongue may with a mortal touch Throw death upon thy sovereign's enemies.
sourceLines: And when they from thy bosom pluck a flower,
Guard it, I pray thee, with a lurking adder
Whose double tongue may with a mortal touch
Throw death upon thy sovereign's enemies.

entries.text: Mock not my senseless conjuration, lords: This earth shall have a feeling and these stones Prove armed soldiers, ere her native king Shall falter under foul rebellion's arms.
sourceLines: Mock not my senseless conjuration, lords:
This earth shall have a feeling and these stones
Prove armed soldiers, ere her native king
Shall falter under foul rebellion's arms.

entries.text: Fear not, my lord: that Power that made you king Hath power to keep you king in spite of all.
sourceLines: Fear not, my lord: that Power that made you king
Hath power to keep you king in spite of all.

entries.text: The means that heaven yields must be embraced, And not neglected; else, if heaven would, And we will not, heaven's offer we refuse, The proffer'd means of succor and redress.
sourceLines: The means that heaven yields must be embraced,
And not neglected; else, if heaven would,
And we will not, heaven's offer we refuse,
The proffer'd means of succor and redress.

entries.text: He means, my lord, that we are too remiss; Whilst Bolingbroke, through our security, Grows strong and great in substance and in power.
sourceLines: He means, my lord, that we are too remiss;
Whilst Bolingbroke, through our security,
Grows strong and great in substance and in power.

entries.text: Discomfortable cousin!
sourceLines: Discomfortable cousin! know'st thou not

entries.text: know'st thou not That when the searching eye of heaven is hid, Behind the globe, that lights the lower world, Then thieves and robbers range abroad unseen In murders and in outrage, boldly here;
sourceLines: Discomfortable cousin! know'st thou not
That when the searching eye of heaven is hid,
Behind the globe, that lights the lower world,
Then thieves and robbers range abroad unseen
In murders and in outrage, boldly here;

entries.text: But when from under this terrestrial ball He fires the proud tops of the eastern pines And darts his light through every guilty hole, Then murders, treasons and detested sins, The cloak of night being pluck'd from off their backs, Stand bare and naked, trembling at themselves?
sourceLines: But when from under this terrestrial ball
He fires the proud tops of the eastern pines
And darts his light through every guilty hole,
Then murders, treasons and detested sins,
The cloak of night being pluck'd from off their backs,
Stand bare and naked, trembling at themselves?

entries.text: So when this thief, this traitor, Bolingbroke, Who all this while hath revell'd in the night Whilst we were wandering with the antipodes, Shall see us rising in our throne, the east, His treasons will sit blushing in his face, Not able to endure the sight of day, But self-affrighted tremble at his sin.
sourceLines: So when this thief, this traitor, Bolingbroke,
Who all this while hath revell'd in the night
Whilst we were wandering with the antipodes,
Shall see us rising in our throne, the east,
His treasons will sit blushing in his face,
Not able to endure the sight of day,
But self-affrighted tremble at his sin.

entries.text: Not all the water in the rough rude sea Can wash the balm off from an anointed king; The breath of worldly men cannot depose The deputy elected by the Lord:
sourceLines: Not all the water in the rough rude sea
Can wash the balm off from an anointed king;
The breath of worldly men cannot depose
The deputy elected by the Lord:

entries.text: For every man that Bolingbroke hath press'd To lift shrewd steel against our golden crown, God for his Richard hath in heavenly pay A glorious angel:
sourceLines: For every man that Bolingbroke hath press'd
To lift shrewd steel against our golden crown,
God for his Richard hath in heavenly pay
A glorious angel: then, if angels fight,

entries.text: Enter EARL OF SALISBURY
then, if angels fight, Weak men must fall, for heaven still guards the right.
sourceLines: A glorious angel: then, if angels fight,
Weak men must fall, for heaven still guards the right.

entries.text: Welcome, my lord how far off lies your power?
sourceLines: Welcome, my lord how far off lies your power?

entries.text: Nor near nor farther off, my gracious lord, Than this weak arm: discomfort guides my tongue And bids me speak of nothing but despair.
sourceLines: Nor near nor farther off, my gracious lord,
Than this weak arm: discomfort guides my tongue
And bids me speak of nothing but despair.

entries.text: One day too late, I fear me, noble lord, Hath clouded all thy happy days on earth: O, call back yesterday, bid time return, And thou shalt have twelve thousand fighting men!
sourceLines: One day too late, I fear me, noble lord,
Hath clouded all thy happy days on earth:
O, call back yesterday, bid time return,
And thou shalt have twelve thousand fighting men!

entries.text: To-day, to-day, unhappy day, too late, O'erthrows thy joys, friends, fortune and thy state: For all the Welshmen, hearing thou wert dead.
sourceLines: To-day, to-day, unhappy day, too late,
O'erthrows thy joys, friends, fortune and thy state:
For all the Welshmen, hearing thou wert dead.

entries.text: Are gone to Bolingbroke, dispersed and fled.
sourceLines: Are gone to Bolingbroke, dispersed and fled.

entries.text: Comfort, my liege; why looks your grace so pale?
sourceLines: Comfort, my liege; why looks your grace so pale?

entries.text: But now the blood of twenty thousand men Did triumph in my face, and they are fled; And, till so much blood thither come again, Have I not reason to look pale and dead?
sourceLines: But now the blood of twenty thousand men
Did triumph in my face, and they are fled;
And, till so much blood thither come again,
Have I not reason to look pale and dead?

entries.text: All souls that will be safe fly from my side, For time hath set a blot upon my pride.
sourceLines: All souls that will be safe fly from my side,
For time hath set a blot upon my pride.

entries.text: Comfort, my liege; remember who you are.
sourceLines: Comfort, my liege; remember who you are.

entries.text: I had forgot myself; am I not king?
sourceLines: I had forgot myself; am I not king?

entries.text: Awake, thou coward majesty! thou sleepest.
sourceLines: Awake, thou coward majesty! thou sleepest.

entries.text: Is not the king's name twenty thousand names?
sourceLines: Is not the king's name twenty thousand names?

entries.text: Arm, arm, my name! a puny subject strikes At thy great glory.
sourceLines: Arm, arm, my name! a puny subject strikes
At thy great glory. Look not to the ground,

entries.text: Look not to the ground, Ye favourites of a king: are we not high?
sourceLines: At thy great glory. Look not to the ground,
Ye favourites of a king: are we not high?

entries.text: High be our thoughts: I know my uncle York Hath power enough to serve our turn.
sourceLines: High be our thoughts: I know my uncle York
Hath power enough to serve our turn. But who comes here?

entries.text: Enter SIR STEPHEN SCROOP
But who comes here?
sourceLines: Hath power enough to serve our turn. But who comes here?

entries.text: More health and happiness betide my liege Than can my care-tuned tongue deliver him!
sourceLines: More health and happiness betide my liege
Than can my care-tuned tongue deliver him!

entries.text: Mine ear is open and my heart prepared; The worst is worldly loss thou canst unfold.
sourceLines: Mine ear is open and my heart prepared;
The worst is worldly loss thou canst unfold.

entries.text: Say, is my kingdom lost?
sourceLines: Say, is my kingdom lost? why, 'twas my care

entries.text: why, 'twas my care And what loss is it to be rid of care?
sourceLines: Say, is my kingdom lost? why, 'twas my care
And what loss is it to be rid of care?

entries.text: Strives Bolingbroke to be as great as we?
sourceLines: Strives Bolingbroke to be as great as we?

entries.text: Greater he shall not be; if he serve God, We'll serve Him too and be his fellow so: Revolt our subjects?
sourceLines: Greater he shall not be; if he serve God,
We'll serve Him too and be his fellow so:
Revolt our subjects? that we cannot mend;

entries.text: that we cannot mend; They break their faith to God as well as us: Cry woe, destruction, ruin and decay: The worst is death, and death will have his day.
sourceLines: Revolt our subjects? that we cannot mend;
They break their faith to God as well as us:
Cry woe, destruction, ruin and decay:
The worst is death, and death will have his day.

entries.text: Glad am I that your highness is so arm'd To bear the tidings of calamity.
sourceLines: Glad am I that your highness is so arm'd
To bear the tidings of calamity.

entries.text: Like an unseasonable stormy day, Which makes the silver rivers drown their shores, As if the world were all dissolved to tears, So high above his limits swells the rage Of Bolingbroke, covering your fearful land With hard bright steel and hearts harder than steel.
sourceLines: Like an unseasonable stormy day,
Which makes the silver rivers drown their shores,
As if the world were all dissolved to tears,
So high above his limits swells the rage
Of Bolingbroke, covering your fearful land
With hard bright steel and hearts harder than steel.

entries.text: White-beards have arm'd their thin and hairless scalps Against thy majesty; boys, with women's voices, Strive to speak big and clap their female joints In stiff unwieldy arms against thy crown:
sourceLines: White-beards have arm'd their thin and hairless scalps
Against thy majesty; boys, with women's voices,
Strive to speak big and clap their female joints
In stiff unwieldy arms against thy crown:

entries.text: The very beadsmen learn to bend their bows Of double-fatal yew against thy state; Yea, distaff-women manage rusty bills Against thy seat:
sourceLines: The very beadsmen learn to bend their bows
Of double-fatal yew against thy state;
Yea, distaff-women manage rusty bills
Against thy seat: both young and old rebel,

entries.text: both young and old rebel, And all goes worse than I have power to tell.
sourceLines: Against thy seat: both young and old rebel,
And all goes worse than I have power to tell.

entries.text: Too well, too well thou tell'st a tale so ill.
sourceLines: Too well, too well thou tell'st a tale so ill.

entries.text: Where is the Earl of Wiltshire?
sourceLines: Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? where is Bagot?

entries.text: where is Bagot?
sourceLines: Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? where is Bagot?

entries.text: What is become of Bushy?
sourceLines: What is become of Bushy? where is Green?

entries.text: where is Green?
sourceLines: What is become of Bushy? where is Green?

entries.text: That they have let the dangerous enemy Measure our confines with such peaceful steps?
sourceLines: That they have let the dangerous enemy
Measure our confines with such peaceful steps?

entries.text: If we prevail, their heads shall pay for it: I warrant they have made peace with Bolingbroke.
sourceLines: If we prevail, their heads shall pay for it:
I warrant they have made peace with Bolingbroke.

entries.text: Peace have they made with him indeed, my lord.
sourceLines: Peace have they made with him indeed, my lord.

entries.text: O villains, vipers, damn'd without redemption!
sourceLines: O villains, vipers, damn'd without redemption!

entries.text: Dogs, easily won to fawn on any man! Snakes, in my heart-blood warm'd, that sting my heart!
sourceLines: Dogs, easily won to fawn on any man!
Snakes, in my heart-blood warm'd, that sting my heart!

entries.text: Three Judases, each one thrice worse than Judas!
sourceLines: Three Judases, each one thrice worse than Judas!

entries.text: Would they make peace?
sourceLines: Would they make peace? terrible hell make war

entries.text: terrible hell make war Upon their spotted souls for this offence!
sourceLines: Would they make peace? terrible hell make war
Upon their spotted souls for this offence!

entries.text: Sweet love, I see, changing his property, Turns to the sourest and most deadly hate: Again uncurse their souls; their peace is made With heads, and not with hands;
sourceLines: Sweet love, I see, changing his property,
Turns to the sourest and most deadly hate:
Again uncurse their souls; their peace is made
With heads, and not with hands; those whom you curse

entries.text: those whom you curse Have felt the worst of death's destroying wound And lie full low, graved in the hollow ground.
sourceLines: With heads, and not with hands; those whom you curse
Have felt the worst of death's destroying wound
And lie full low, graved in the hollow ground.

entries.text: Is Bushy, Green, and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?
sourceLines: Is Bushy, Green, and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?

entries.text: Ay, all of them at Bristol lost their heads.
sourceLines: Ay, all of them at Bristol lost their heads.

entries.text: Where is the duke my father with his power?
sourceLines: Where is the duke my father with his power?

entries.text: No matter where; of comfort no man speak: Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;
sourceLines: No matter where; of comfort no man speak:
Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;

entries.text: Make dust our paper and with rainy eyes Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth, Let's choose executors and talk of wills:
sourceLines: Make dust our paper and with rainy eyes
Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth,
Let's choose executors and talk of wills:

entries.text: And yet not so, for what can we bequeath Save our deposed bodies to the ground?
sourceLines: And yet not so, for what can we bequeath
Save our deposed bodies to the ground?

entries.text: Our lands, our lives and all are Bolingbroke's, And nothing can we call our own but death And that small model of the barren earth Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.
sourceLines: Our lands, our lives and all are Bolingbroke's,
And nothing can we call our own but death
And that small model of the barren earth
Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.

entries.text: For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground And tell sad stories of the death of kings; How some have been deposed; some slain in war, Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;
sourceLines: For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground
And tell sad stories of the death of kings;
How some have been deposed; some slain in war,
Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;

entries.text: Some poison'd by their wives: some sleeping kill'd; All murder'd:
sourceLines: Some poison'd by their wives: some sleeping kill'd;
All murder'd: for within the hollow crown

entries.text: for within the hollow crown That rounds the mortal temples of a king Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits, Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp, Allowing him a breath, a little scene, To monarchize, be fear'd and kill with looks, Infusing him with self and vain conceit, As if this flesh which walls about our life, Were brass impregnable, and humour'd thus Comes at the last and with a little pin Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!
sourceLines: All murder'd: for within the hollow crown
That rounds the mortal temples of a king
Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits,
Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
Allowing him a breath, a little scene,
To monarchize, be fear'd and kill with looks,
Infusing him with self and vain conceit,
As if this flesh which walls about our life,
Were brass impregnable, and humour'd thus
Comes at the last and with a little pin
Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!

entries.text: Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood With solemn reverence: throw away respect, Tradition, form and ceremonious duty, For you have but mistook me all this while:
sourceLines: Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood
With solemn reverence: throw away respect,
Tradition, form and ceremonious duty,
For you have but mistook me all this while:

entries.text: I live with bread like you, feel want, Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus, How can you say to me, I am a king?
sourceLines: I live with bread like you, feel want,
Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus,
How can you say to me, I am a king?

entries.text: My lord, wise men ne'er sit and wail their woes, But presently prevent the ways to wail.
sourceLines: My lord, wise men ne'er sit and wail their woes,
But presently prevent the ways to wail.

entries.text: To fear the foe, since fear oppresseth strength, Gives in your weakness strength unto your foe, And so your follies fight against yourself.
sourceLines: To fear the foe, since fear oppresseth strength,
Gives in your weakness strength unto your foe,
And so your follies fight against yourself.

entries.text: Fear and be slain; no worse can come to fight: And fight and die is death destroying death; Where fearing dying pays death servile breath.
sourceLines: Fear and be slain; no worse can come to fight:
And fight and die is death destroying death;
Where fearing dying pays death servile breath.

entries.text: My father hath a power; inquire of him And learn to make a body of a limb.
sourceLines: My father hath a power; inquire of him
And learn to make a body of a limb.

entries.text: Thou chidest me well: proud Bolingbroke, I come To change blows with thee for our day of doom.
sourceLines: Thou chidest me well: proud Bolingbroke, I come
To change blows with thee for our day of doom.

entries.text: This ague fit of fear is over-blown; An easy task it is to win our own.
sourceLines: This ague fit of fear is over-blown;
An easy task it is to win our own.

entries.text: Say, Scroop, where lies our uncle with his power?
sourceLines: Say, Scroop, where lies our uncle with his power?

entries.text: Speak sweetly, man, although thy looks be sour.
sourceLines: Speak sweetly, man, although thy looks be sour.

entries.text: Men judge by the complexion of the sky The state and inclination of the day: So may you by my dull and heavy eye, My tongue hath but a heavier tale to say.
sourceLines: Men judge by the complexion of the sky
The state and inclination of the day:
So may you by my dull and heavy eye,
My tongue hath but a heavier tale to say.

entries.text: I play the torturer, by small and small To lengthen out the worst that must be spoken:
sourceLines: I play the torturer, by small and small
To lengthen out the worst that must be spoken:

entries.text: Your uncle York is join'd with Bolingbroke, And all your northern castles yielded up, And all your southern gentlemen in arms Upon his party.
sourceLines: Your uncle York is join'd with Bolingbroke,
And all your northern castles yielded up,
And all your southern gentlemen in arms
Upon his party.

entries.text: Thou hast said enough.
sourceLines: Thou hast said enough.

entries.text: To DUKE OF AUMERLE
Beshrew thee, cousin, which didst lead me forth
sourceLines: Beshrew thee, cousin, which didst lead me forth

entries.text: Of that sweet way I was in to despair! What say you now?
sourceLines: Of that sweet way I was in to despair!
What say you now? what comfort have we now?

entries.text: what comfort have we now?
sourceLines: What say you now? what comfort have we now?

entries.text: By heaven, I'll hate him everlastingly That bids me be of comfort any more.
sourceLines: By heaven, I'll hate him everlastingly
That bids me be of comfort any more.

entries.text: Go to Flint castle: there I'll pine away; A king, woe's slave, shall kingly woe obey.
sourceLines: Go to Flint castle: there I'll pine away;
A king, woe's slave, shall kingly woe obey.

entries.text: That power I have, discharge; and let them go To ear the land that hath some hope to grow, For I have none: let no man speak again To alter this, for counsel is but vain.
sourceLines: That power I have, discharge; and let them go
To ear the land that hath some hope to grow,
For I have none: let no man speak again
To alter this, for counsel is but vain.

entries.text: My liege, one word.
sourceLines: My liege, one word.

entries.text: He does me double wrong That wounds me with the flatteries of his tongue.
sourceLines: He does me double wrong
That wounds me with the flatteries of his tongue.

entries.text: Exeunt
Discharge my followers: let them hence away, From Richard's night to Bolingbroke's fair day.
sourceLines: Discharge my followers: let them hence away,
From Richard's night to Bolingbroke's fair day.
